fascist ideology, human persuadability, revolutionary unconscious, critical pedagogy, critical psychoanalysis, critical relationality

Seeking to frame the debate around academic freedom in terms of freedom of thought, this article begins with an exploration of the hazards of fascist ideology and the psychodynamics of persuadability. Attention is paid to the perverse lure of certainty and the apparent willingness of many people to accede to an instrumentalized unconscious. Through the writings of Butler and Athanasiou, an antithesis to the dispossession of an instrumentalized unconscious is explored in terms of radical performativity and critical relationality, modalities which have the potential to undo what Elizabeth Povinelli termed “the cunning of recognition.” The limitations of psychoanalysis due to its historical antecedents in colonialism and racialized capitalism are explored, and an argument for a genealogically and sociohistorically constituted psychoanalysis is entertained. Following Derrida's imagining of the university as truth-seeker, aspects of the history of U.S. higher education are explored to illustrate the continuous struggle between sovereign power and capitalist logic and the possibility of education as the practice of freedom. The essay concludes with an exploration of the intersection between psychoanalysis and critical pedagogy, posing the question of whether analytic institutes and universities might become vehicles for an encounter with alterity that could potentially sow the seeds for a revolutionary unconscious.

This paper focusses on a series of online attacks that the author was subjected to after comments he had made in a closed lecture on the topic of ‘white anxiety’ were cut from the zoom recording and distributed widely online with the clear intent of causing outrage. The analysis of the material, which combines thematic, discourse analytic and personal reflections, yielded a series of core themes: 1) the role of the messages in consolidating an identity, 2) performative offensiveness, 3) perverse intimidations, 4) accusations/denials/expressions of racism, 5) the race- traitor as ideological dilemma, 6) antisemitism and 7) aggressive cordiality. The paper closes with a few reflections on the author's enunciative position in respect of the attacks.

The essay interrogates the history and contemporary plight of academic freedom in the current context of heightened political pressures amidst polarizing, moralizing ideological commitments and suppressions of free inquiry, debate, dissent, and truth seeking. It argues that such semiotic collapses reflect a vanishing signifying gap, which has unconscious determinants linked with the erasures of the feminine, and which produces a stifling insistence on sameness at the expense of difference. By examining the surveillances of speech in the context of Israel- Palestine, and particularly post October 7, the essays argues that Palestine, as the site of radical rupture of the signifying chain, occupies a space where freedom of association and speech halt. This crisis also functions as a zero point to law, a semiotic and structural role occupied by the feminine and its cryptic yet spatializing signified, the vaginal. When enabled, this signifying gap opens an onto-ethical space between the real of ancestral, disavowed trauma and the symbolic discursive realm, revealing unsettling truths, social tensions, and liberatory desires. Its relevance to the semiotic confinements and censorial campaigns haunting the academy (and general culture) but also haunting the holy contested land, occupied territories, and contiguous/noncontiguous borders of Israel-Palestine is not accidental; perhaps this void is so primal as to be barely a metaphor for the sacred dimensions between possession and dispossession essential to political, semiotic, and spiritual liberation/ enfranchisement. The wave of encampments and protests across US campuses, unsettling and agitating as they necessarily must be, underscore the primacy of the gap, of a symbolic and real space, in fostering a mutually constitutive relationship between academic freedom and emancipatory politics.

This paper elucidates the work of science and technology studies (STS) feminists Donna Haraway and Karen Barad as their theories relate to the production of matter, agency, and knowledge in psychotherapy. Haraway's and Barad's work center on questions of epistemology and highlight the ontological and ethical dimensions of knowledge production. Haraway and Barad articulate a diffractive methodology which attends to the situatedness of knowledge and the materiality of perception, articulating the conditions for an ontological-epistemological-ethical entanglement which situates agency in the entanglement as a whole. I will begin by illuminating this aspect of their work, which will then be interwoven with the life of another STS feminist, my patient Marianna. My clinical entanglement with their work will borrow and hopefully resonate with the focus of this special issue on academic freedom.

Tunisia has a middling rank on the Academic Freedom Index and, in 2017, a Tunisian University Charter was created. Despite that, many symptoms show the withering of academic freedom. This paper proposes a psychoanalytical reading within a multifactorial hostility to the implementation of academic freedom in Tunisia. I present this account from my own trial by fire as a Tunisian woman, academic and researcher in a scientifically “peripheral” country struggling with what I call “the epistemology of Procrustes's bed”. A holistic understanding of the hindrances to academic freedom may contribute to its democratization and to ethical and equitable science.

Julie Reshe's book, Negative Psychoanalysis for the Living Dead, stands out as an exceptional and unconventional work in the realm of psychoanalytic literature. It has swiftly become a subject of widespread discussion and interest, capturing the attention of many. This book diverges from traditional norms in several key aspects. It is explicitly stated as not being “recommended for anyone.” In her interviews, Reshe cautions that readers might regret engaging with its contents. However, the experience of reading it often proves to be the opposite—akin to finding a friend who is willing to listen patiently to one's deepest grief and darkest musings. The book's defining characteristic is its refusal to offer salvation or aspire to clarify or improve anything. Reshe posits that proposing salvation or improvement inherently involves a denial of life's darker aspects. The book appears to assume the role of a listener rather than that of a speaker, creating a space of understanding rather than providing guidance.

In her earlier work on depressive realism, Reshe highlights the stigma often associated with the voice of depression. Through her book, it seems she is destigmatizing this voice, offering it legitimacy and understanding. She admits that the exploration of human existence in her book centers around a fundamentally depressed being. She reconsiders depression and negative states not as deviations from our natural state, but as an intrinsic quality of human existence. Instead of treating them as distorted or inadequate perceptions of the world, Reshe views them as a form of attunement to our existence and the existence of the world. This book offers no consolation; rather, it posits that conventional forms of consolation, be they religious or therapeutic, often serve as mechanisms for denying crucial aspects of human existence.

The readers of this journal could be forgiven for never having heard of IPE, a subdivision of international relations that explores economic power in a globalised world, and that typically lags a decade or two behind other disciplines in its engagement with the latest developments in critical theory. The work edited by Paola Bohórquez and Verónica Garibotto aims to address the role played by psychoanalysis in different contexts in Latin America and the Caribbean, but without limiting itself to just classic private-consultation psychoanalysis or the psychoanalyst locked in their consulting room receiving patients from a certain socioeconomic stratum. On the contrary, it seeks to disseminate the diverse and original ways in which psychoanalysis can be thought of from different perspectives. The point is to put psychoanalysis in dialogue with other fields of knowledge, such as sociology, anthropology, cultural and gender studies, and philosophy. Overall, the book seems to want to answer a question: how can psychoanalysis be used to understand contemporary psychic suffering in a part of the world where the diversity of sexualities, races, and classes has historically been used as a basis for segregation and rejection? Categories such as race, gender, and class come to be questioned in some of the chapters, suggesting the beginning of a type of decolonization of the discourse. The book is divided into three sections: the first explores the sociopolitical readings psychoanalysis can offer on different social issues; the second delves into themes intersecting with psychoanalysis, and considers how it is used and hosted in different countries; and the third section offers a more historical approach to psychoanalysis in Latin America, including a chapter on the history of the Argentine Psychoanalytic Association and the journal, Revista de Psicoanálisis. I will present what, in my opinion, are the chapters to highlight and that deserve attention, and conclude with a reading and analysis of the two most representative chapters of the book.

Lower caste demographics experience an infringed relationship with freedom itself. Through private interviews with nine American academic psychoanalysts, this author discovered consistent themes of silencing, exclusion and emotional toll. In this paper, abyssal positioning is applied to capture the differential experiences of academic freedom of expression. Because a purist psychoanalytic framing can be exclusive and narrowing, as was suggested by many of the participants, critical race theory, research from social psychology, and psychoanalytic constructs are interwoven to frame the unconscious motivations that keep these dynamics status quo. Radical examples of reparative and liberatory actions are offered.

Can the non-white speak? Who can express themselves on the analyst’s couch and in what terms? How does the inscription of the subject and the subject of the unconscious in social relations of power of race limit the access to analytical elaboration? Psychoanalysis appears as one of the last products of modernity, and just as it emerged within the deployment of sexuality, it also developed within the founding of coloniality and capitalism in the modern era. While it can fundamentally question various aspects of the capitalist system or the deployment of sexuality, it most often exempts itself from the study of coloniality within its clinical or theoretical apparatus. Giving a voice, creating a space for singular voices remains one of the aims of psychoanalytic listening. How, then, can a space be created for othered voices, indigenous voices silenced by the processes of colonial re-actualisation, and how can memories and their current effects be retrieved? What effects can the social denial of race have here? To ask who can speak in psychoanalysis and in what terms entails examining whether there is not a specific racial form of subjective silencing, distinct from Freudian repression or language alienation, and to what extent it happens to be perpetuated in the analyst’s practice. What social silencing, imposed on the conscious and unconscious experiences and representations of racialised analysands, is reproduced in the analyst’s practice, when they listen from an invisibilised, because supposedly universal, position, and thus become deaf to the specificity of the analysand’s racial experience? What are the effects of whiteness on the psychic processes of analysts and analysands, how is it imposed as a subjectivation norm and how does it consequently foreclose discursive multiplicity? The aim here is to shed light on the impact of race and whiteness in psychoanalysis, and analyse their role in symbolic transference, using standpoint epistemologies and the epistemology of ignorance.

This paper addresses unique intersectional identities within the Muslim community, and some common assumptions regarding “religious identity” and the blind spots that this creates in the therapeutic space. It discusses the author’s advocacy work for queer Muslims seeking an identity or cultural match with a Muslim therapist who also affirms their queer identities, and explores issues related to invisible and visible identities, intersectionality, belonging, and advocacy. This paper uses intersectionality as a framework to emphasize the added labor, adversity and invisible negotiations that Muslims who do not fit the stereotype “Muslim” face from all angles. Applying Jasbir Puar’s conceptualization of “homonationalism,” which captures the multiple negotiations queer Muslims living in the west face as they also navigate their other intersecting identities, this paper argues that the invisibility of some identities creates both barriers to mental health care and the potential for secret solidarity between provider and client. The reader is brought on a journey of secret solidarity—the bond formed between those who understand the risk of allying with queerness as a Muslim person, and the lengths we all go to be perceived a certain way while trying to make revolutionary change.

The Covid-19 pandemic seems strangely absent present. In a sense, the intense period of lockdowns, spiralling death figures, infections, restrictions and unprecedented psychosocial change in many parts of the world seems behind us and long gone. Even though the pandemic began at some point in December 2019 and the WHO officially ended its designation as a ‘public health emergency of international concern’ in May 2023, it seems to have been overshadowed recently by the war in Ukraine, a new level of escalation in the Israel-Palestine conflict and other global events. The ‘new normal’ is yesterday’s news. Yet, it has left a lasting legacy on many aspects of life we have learnt, or not learnt, to live with. Above all, at its height, Covid-19 changed human relationships and psychodynamics. As people stayed at home and face-to-face life seemingly stood still, they turned to screens and were then truly ‘together alone’, as Sherry Turkle (2021) put it in an article for Time magazine, flipping her famous diagnosis of our technologically-saturated lives. As events, talks, weddings and even funerals moved online and were streamed via software such as Zoom, the internet offered many a sense of feeling connected yet also alienated, alone, vulnerable or anxious of what was to come.

What is greed? This interesting and wide-ranging book takes us through some key debates with a red thread argument, that it is necessary to develop a form of psychoanalytic Marxism. In this project, and to take forward this agenda, it is often the questions that are more revealing than the actual answers. There are some heavy assumptions here about the universality of psychoanalytic descriptions of subjectivity and, towards the end of the book, some much heavier-going explication of Marxist economics. The economics is key to the argument, and Johnston holds to a particular political-theoretic tradition in Marxism that he defends with gusto, aiming to meld it with a particular tradition of work in psychoanalysis and Lacanian theory, so as to arrive at something he dubs ‘Lacano-Marxism’ (p. 1). So, there are two aspects to the issue of greed that Johnston wants to treat as different angles on the same thing, angles that are compatible, complementary even, potentially conjoined.

On the one hand, and this is a real contribution of the book, there is a focus on the structurally-embedded nature of ‘greed’ under capitalism, a second nature that then embeds itself in each singular subject, subjects us to it in such a way that it appears to rise up from within the self. The formula for this greed is given us by Marx to describe the capital flow from money (M) to the production of a commodity (C) and then, from sale of that commodity, to an enhanced form of money (M′). The circuit M-C-M′ is a critique of capitalism, for the ‘value’ that appears at the end of the circuit is there by virtue of the ‘surplus value’ that the capitalist has extracted from the labour of a worker, a worker who has been forced, under only-apparently free contract, to sell their labour power for a period of time and has, within that time, worked above and beyond what is necessary. That is time stolen by the capitalism, exploitation concealed and profit harvested when objects that could have ‘use value’ are turned into commodities that, on the marketplace, have mere ‘exchange value’.

Noting with Octave Mannoni and Frantz Fanon the nihilistic temptation to produce a world without humans in the dying colonial world, Aimé Césaire associated the colonial psychology that made this temptation possible with that which fascism/nazism had produced in Europe at the same time. By re-examining Wilhelm Reich's proposal concerning the mass psychology of fascism, this article looks at why the superego is not a psychoanalytic concept mobilized by the first wave of Freudo-Marxism, and what use could be made of it anyway to measure the political effects of the alliance between Superego and death drive.

This paper explores the integration of Julia Kristeva’s concept of abjection into the sociology of knowledge, with a particular focus on the cultural phenomenon of hyperrealistic sex dolls. Employing a unique methodological approach, this paper interprets Kristeva’s Powers of Horror through Berger and Luckmann’s The Social Construction of Reality by utilizing two observation-based vignettes. It proposes a novel translation of the abject, typically a psychoanalytic concept, into empirical research frameworks that traditionally emphasize everyday reality. This synthesis extends the boundaries of a sociology of knowledge by incorporating affective responses to transgressive phenomena. The findings suggest that pre-recognition psychoanalytic concepts can significantly broaden the theoretical scope of sociology, offering new lenses to examine events and affects that lie beyond conventional sociological analysis.

Using data collected from participant observation through creative workshops in two regions of the UK in 2019 and 2020 with participants going through the asylum system, this paper seeks to redress the under-theorisation of Axel Honneth’s use of critical and psychoanalytic theory including the work of Donald Winnicott within Honneth’s book The Struggle for Recognition. Crucially, this approach sees Honneth’s primary intersubjective process of recognition, love, as ambivalent, as opposed to monolithically conceived, a common criticism of Honneth’s early work, and applies this conception to empirical data. Following the work of philosopher Amy Allen, this paper also resolves to apply Jessica Benjamin’s use of the Third to a number of empirical case studies relating to creative workshops conducted with participants going through the asylum system. By taking this ambivalent approach, this paper shows how meaningful recognition might more successfully be achieved beyond the limits of such the punitive regimes of asylum.

Psychoanalysis, Colonialism, Coloniality, Colonization, Decolonization, Decoloniality

This paper introduces the special issue on psychoanalysis and colonialism. As guest editors we also offer our own contribution to the topic. First, we connect the history of psychoanalysis with that of colonialism and distinguish concepts such as colonialism, coloniality, decolonization and decoloniality, as well as three perspectives on coloniality: Postcolonial theory, the decolonial turn, and the anticolonial struggle. Then we recapitulate psychoanalysis’s approaches to colonialism and coloniality, starting with Sigmund Freud’s ideas on primitivism, continuing with the psychoanalytic apologies for colonialism and delving into Freudian traces in the works of Oswald de Andrade, René Ménil, Wulf Sachs, Octave Mannoni, Frantz Fanon, Santiago Ramírez, Albert Memmi, Édouard Glissant, Ashis Nandy, Homi Bhabha, Edward Said, and current authors. Finally, we discuss colonial features, effects and uses of psychoanalysis, before moving on to summarize and comment on the articles included in this special issue.

He is an activist, psychotherapist, farmer, union organizer with the Massachusetts State College Association, small-town newspaper recipe columnist, and pain in the neck.
Psychoanalytic institutes, Psychoanalysis, Academic freedom, Discrimination, Authoritarianism

American psychoanalytic institute culture is fundamentally hostile to academic freedom, and to the scholarly and cultural norms that can promote it! I offer three illustrative vignettes as cases in point. I then extensively review the available historical, ethnographic, survey, interview, and anecdotal evidence for the claim that American psychoanalytic institutes are hostile to academic freedom by design, while offering an analysis of why this hostility to academic freedom has served the authoritarian interests of charismatic leaders in psychoanalysis. I conclude with some brief comments on what would need to change in the institutional structures, practices, and faculties of American psychoanalytic institutes to make them more amenable to academic freedom.

This article uses a scholarly case to analyze how psychoanalytic soft power is extended to govern and regulate the “psychic sovereignty” of “non-normative” subjects, especially racialized, gendered and sexualized subjects in, from and of the Global South. In using an example from the ways psychoanalysis circulates within France (in particular within contemporary debates of what constitutes someone who is truly “French”), we consider how the “French intellectual tradition” mobilizes -despite its critique of them–universalizing concepts of secularism and citizenry to shore up, what we call, the colonial republic of psychoanalysis. Psychoanalysis itself is a formation that collaborates and colludes with colonial power (especially in its most liberal form) through its claim to the right over the psychic sovereignty of both individuals and nations who are in proximity to French colonial and neocolonial rule. Through close critique of the recent work of Élisabeth Roudinesco (and a handful of others) as a generalized but accurate case study, this article considers how psychoanalysis and psychoanalysts police sovereignty and “innocently” lodge themselves in liberal state discourse to control, manage and designate what psyches, bodies and subjects are deserving of empathy, rights, and psychological consideration. We explore how psychoanalysis as a normative method and practice designates who is perverse and who is deviant, who are genuinely good and bad objects, and is worthy of saving or worthy of expelling.

Drawing on a scan of psychoanalytic writing, this paper engages with the historical absence of race as a subject of enquiry within classical psychoanalytic thinking and practice. In considering that psychoanalysis has only recently begun to engage more intentionally with race in thinking and practice, we suggest that this engagement has historically been complicated, and remains complex, because it challenges foundational psychoanalytic tenets, whilst concomitantly provoking a jeopardy of the self of the analyst/therapist. The paper distills key conceptual issues that are contested when considering the relevance of the racialized societal landscape on the development of the psyche—in particular, the impact on conceptualizing the nature of the unconscious, and of transference and countertransference. In addition, we consider the question of analytic neutrality and the manner in which racial melancholia may manifest to generate vulnerabilities for the analyst/therapist, when race is central to the analytic encounter. The paper emerges from an assumption that the internal world is not quarantined from external social discourses, practices and structures, but rather that these are reciprocally implicated in the structuring of the psyche. We propose a psychoanalytic project that engages with the psychic imprint of the external world, and allows for the possibility that the resolution of racial entanglements may not be the therapeutic ideal, and that ongoing work with such ambivalences and contradictions may in fact be desirable.

antisemitism, whiteness, racism, academic freedom

In the furore over Derek Hook's article ‘White Anxiety’ and Donald Moss's ‘On Having Whiteness’, an under-reported but important issue is how easily and strongly antisemitism surfaced. Derek Hook is not Jewish but was assumed to be so by some of his abusive critics on the grounds probably that no white person would make the kinds of statements he was alleged to make (themselves, of course, a distortion of his actual article). Moss is Jewish, which makes it easier for his critics to see him as an adversary; not so much a ‘race traitor’ as a Jew who has relinquished his provisional whiteness. In both cases, one issue amongst the many to do with ‘academic freedom’ is how and why the racialisation of hatred can occur so strongly, often as antisemitism, in the context of psychoanalytic explorations of racism and especially of whiteness.

In ‘Mochlos; or, The Conflict of the Faculties’, Jacques Derrida critiques the topography of the inside and the outside of the modern university and proposes the margin as a possible locus of responsibility and truth from which an academic could speak. In States of Shock, Bernard Stiegler considers the shifts in economics, knowledge production and communication that the modern university must address. Us-ness, Pre-subject, Processes of subjectivation, Ontological vulnerability, Restorative justice

This paper examines the backdrop of safety from which one’s sense of “I-ness” emerges, building on Winnicott’s assertion that “there’s no such thing as a baby” to explore the implications of the unconscious structure termed “us-ness.” Interpreting Winnicott’s emphasis on the environment as suggesting that the pre-subject (the infant) forms an “us” with the (m)other, I propose that inadequately held dependence at this foundational level is semiotically impressed upon the other—manifesting through action. This interpretation extends to suggest a deeply embedded understanding of the psyche-social dynamic. Within this framework of evolving subjectivity, I argue that the pre-subject requires a subjectivizing other: someone who embraces their role within the relational asymmetry of early dependence, thereby enabling the formation of “us.” This emphasis is further developed to connect with principles of restorative justice, as illustrated in a second vignette that highlights what the concept of justice overlooks by failing to account for the continual processes of subjectivation achieved through profound relational engagement. The paper explores this potential space of becoming, emphasizing that it first necessitates the somatic experience of another, as demonstrated through two vignettes. These vignettes underscore a fundamental human need: to feel acknowledged and taken seriously by another. This need for interoceptive recognition shapes one’s relationship with oneself and with the external world. The transition from an initial silent vulnerability, inherent at birth, into subjecthood depends on the stabilizing presence of another, providing ontological grounding. This grounding imbues the vulnerable dimensions of the subject with a lasting psychic tissue, fostering a sense of security. I argue that this dynamic has profound implications for the subject’s relationship with the social world, as experiences of “us-ness” evolve into an identification with a shared “we.”

This article provides a critique of Martha Nussbaum’s use of Donald Winnicott’s psychoanalysis in the field of political theory. In particular, it shows that Nussbaum omits specific elements in Winnicott’s thinking that may be described as “vitalist”. Nussbaum uses Winnicott’s ideas to justify a teleological view of human maturity which can hardly be harmonised with some of his seminal views of human subjectivity. The paper argues that, despite being true to Winnicott’s theory in many ways, Nussbuam commits a decisive interpretive shift which involves subordinating the Winnicottian “life force” under regulative norms of the liberal political order.

Gal Gerson   Teaches political theory and the history of political thought at the Division of Government and Political Theory, the School of Political Sciences, at the University of Haifa. He is author of several books and articles on the history of liberalism, populism, and psychoanalysis.
Winnicott, Critical theory, Schizoids, Kretschmer

Winnicott is often endorsed by critical theory, primarily because he offers a less rigid approach than orthodox psychoanalysis. He also displays a dialectical feature that matches the Hegelian bent that critical theory retains from its Marxist origins. However, Winnicott also entails some serious exclusions that subvert efforts to enlist him for critical theory. This can be prevalently seen in his attitude to the schizoid condition. He views that condition as both particularly ill and as socially disruptive. At the basis of the schizoid condition, as he understands it, is a sense of detachment from, and hostility towards, the social order—any social order. The schizoid flaw, in other words, resides in being antithetical. If antithesis is cast as the core illness, the Winnicott alliance with critical theory is undermined, rendering aspects of Winnicott’s theory collusive with a normalized status quo.

Play, Creation, Solitude, Potential space

This article argues for the possibility of non-transitional play in an inner potential space cut off from the external world. Therein, the child does not play alone in the presence of someone else, as is the case in Winnicott’s transitional play, but in a radical solitude where he is not mirrored by anyone. It is argued that this hinders the child from feeling that he is someone, and that this “someone” is equal to himself. Instead, the child remains no one, and beyond the reach of the mirror and the symbol. In conversation with Pessoa, Borges, Ibn Arabi, and Rimbaud,  the author proposes that this enables him to create an inner world for himself, and seeing what is unimaginable, thus rendering him a creating seer rather than a subject. Furthermore, it is postulated that the gap between no one and someone draws a line which society cannot cross.

This paper argues for the continuing significance of D. W. Winnicott’s work. A main goal of the paper is to show that Winnicott is especially needed to respond to threats to higher education, especially in the United States context. American politics have been highly charged for several election cycles, and American higher education has come under increased scrutiny if not direct attack. This paper argues that the American public has lost faith in higher education, and that one way to rebuild faith is to engage with Winnicott’s thinking. I am especially interested in the ways that Winnicott helps us push back against influencer culture, making space for the good enough, and appreciating how higher education isn’t just one influence among others. Rather, higher education, when it is working, facilitates student freedom.

The goal of the paper is to study all the implications of Donald W. Winnicott’s definition of democracy as maturity. Why is democracy the only political regime to achieve that which is the goal of human life in general: to go beyond immaturity and its dangers? How does it relate to psychological maturity in general, which human beings have to achieve by themselves in ordinary life? What are the challenges and risks implied (and revealed) by such a definition, since immaturity is a chronic and ever renewing danger in human history? This paper tries to answer these questions through a careful and internal reading of one precise Winnicott article. It allows us to set up and redefine the political frame, the human foundations, and the old and new challenges of democracy as such, which it faces today no less than before.

This is the approach advocated by Robert Samuels in The Psychopathology of Political Ideologies. Samuels’s core thesis is that the stale and ossified dichotomy between Conservative and Liberal, Republican and Democrat, which structures the current political impasse has become a zombie-like antimony that serves to obscure profound differences between five competing ideologies that together constitute the actual driving forces of the contemporary cultural-political scene. Our inability to recognize and appreciate the differences between these five ideological outlooks has impoverished public political discourse and led us to often misperceive the distinct animating bases of both our own and other’s political worldviews. For Samuels, this state of confusion is unsurprising since one reason these political ideologies have become so illegible is that they are each informed by an unconscious fantasy shaping a person’s political outlook. This paper is an exercise in theorizing political subjectivity through the lens of Winnicott and in the context of contemporary workplace politics. While scholars have made considerable traction applying Winnicott’s thinking to work and organizational settings, rarely is political agency and its connection to worker resistance and emancipation explored. This paper argues that Winnicott offers a novel and underappreciated theory of political subjectivity that is both at odds with relational thinking by advocating for a fundamental “incommunicado” element of separateness, and distinct from an inherently mediated (or inscribed) view of subjectivity by allowing for spontaneity and surprise. Specifically, what Winnicott’s theory of political subjectivity offers is a sense of being at ease, or “going-on-being,” that in its most basic sense is a feeling of aliveness that comes in and through the spontaneous gesture. If this view of subjectivity, grounded in Winnicott’s signature concept of the true self, is at once suspect of essentialism and liberal bourgeois individualism, it is also precisely where we must start from in reclaiming a place to truly live. This paper explores how the true self’s unknown, unfound, and forever non-communicating qualities possess a “queer kind of truth” in the face of an impinging neoliberal order, and particularly in a world of work where a fetishized subjectivity, premised on the self’s exploitative use, is at play. Moreover, it is from this vantage that the call for recognition—the goal of much progressive workplace politics—becomes a trap; a way to expose the self to further forms of compliance-ridden exploitation.

Xenophobia is the fear of foreigners. This word is not interchangeable with racism and its manifestations can have enduring ramifications. Although various schools of psychoanalytic thought, including Freudian, Jungian, and Kleinian, have offered explanations for xenophobia, none explain the endopsychic structural changes in the individual during the manifestations of xenophobic behaviors. Fairbairn’s multilayered theory has attracted more attention over the past decades in clinical and non-clinical settings. In this paper, this theory is used to explain the structural alterations that occur as an individual shows xenophobic behavior or manifests a propensity for demagoguery. Furthermore, Fairbairn’s theory of endopsychic structure is used to show what discourses could provoke these dynamics. Finally, there is a suggestion for creating an atmosphere conducive to a more stable psyche for the next generation.

This research proposes a psychoanalytic listening of the Malagasy bilo ritual in its classical form. The ritual’s function is to address the fertility issues of the entire lineage through the medium of the body of a woman described as “infertile” or who has only given birth to daughters. The goal is to fortify the life of a particular lineage, via a woman who will symbolically “give birth to” an ancestor. Our work aims to approach how the ritual accomplishes unconscious desires and processes psychic functions. We rely on the discourse of the work carried out by French anthropologists Fiéloux and Lombard who have studied the ritual most extensively. Five lines of analysis emerged: the central place of the body in the hallucinatory fulfilment of desire, the psychic treatment of femininity and passivity in both men and women, the processing of unconscious hostility, the elaboration of loss, and the projection of superego in the bilo.

This study examines Brazilian racism in relation to the traumatic legacy of slavery, focusing on denial and disavowal as distinct psychic mechanisms. This paper develops a new approach to psychoanalytic media studies by applying the neuropsychoanalytic model of the brain by Mark Solms. It proposes that the conscious id is the driving force behind our social networks online, and that Lacanian real is equivalent to Friston free energy. Using Solms’s model, online experience is theorized, according to the psychoanalytic concepts of Freud and Lacan, between affective consciousness and linguistic consciousness, respectively. This paper aims to provide a socio-psychoanalytic description of the late modern psyche by turning to psychoanalyst Jessica Benjamin and further uniting her theory of intersubjectivity with sociologist Hartmut Rosa’s contemporary analysis. It claims that Western culture is characterized by omnipotence and that a new differentiation of self and world is needed where intersubjectivity must be promoted to create a society that safeguards equality, democracy and ethics. It is proposed that a synthesis of Benjamin’s and Rosa’s theories offer a powerful framework for navigating individual and societal challenges in the pursuit of greater human contact and understanding.

During the last decade, we can observe rising support for right-wing leaders who produce a discourse of semblance of strength. These leaders, the new masters of politics, concentrate on the performance of political charisma and manifest a disregard for the norms of the contemporary public sphere. Using Jacques Lacan’s theory of discourses, this article argues that there is a structural relation between the discontents in neoliberal forms of power and the success of these leaders performing the theatre of charisma and political dominance. The key to understanding the rise of the new masters of politics is the relation between the discourse of the master and that of the university. The political prominence of the new masters of politics can be interpreted as a precise reaction to the form of power dominant in neoliberalism – bureaucracy operating according to the norms of economic rationality. The main aim of this paper is to provide a theoretically informed interpretation of discourses of semblance of strength in the broader frame of the historical moment of a crisis of neoliberal form of power.

I recently encountered a woman and her young grandson in the waiting room of a psychiatric hospital. They were there to see her daughter, the child’s mother. In the midst of telling me about his Minecraft game, the boy deviated, with no encouragement and in an unaffected manner, to the subject of his mother, casually mentioning that she had been taken to hospital because she talked to ghosts. His calm was in contrast to the agitated state of his grandmother, who complained loudly about the wait. The receptionist tried to raise a sympathetic smile – the usual problems with the room booking system. The woman, overwhelmed with dread and confusion, spoke to me a little. A few weeks previously, without precedent, her daughter had been sectioned with psychosis – a radically altered situation for which the family had no map and no frame of reference.

Psychoanalysts will tell you, that in both its noisy and more discreet forms, psychosis is ubiquitous, all the while remaining little understood as a phenomenon. In timely fashion, Lacanian psychoanalyst Stijn Vanheule’s latest book Why Psychosis is Not So Crazy, a resolutely accessible text, seeks to illuminate the experience of psychosis for families and caregivers. In a moment when the psychological investigation of mental suffering has been marginalised, if not foreclosed, by psychiatric services, this is a vital piece of writing.

In the 1970s, a popular appreciation of Lacanian theory took hold in France. The result? Medics, school counsellors and social workers often had a good understanding of psychoanalytic concepts, including ways to conceptualise psychosis. This is not, and has never been, the case in the UK. In the event of a psychosis in the family, the answers that come from mental health services can be of little help. psychodynamic time, asylum seekers, Nachträglichkeit, Hans Loewald, Greece

On the basis of ethnographic evidence obtained during fieldwork in Greece with Afghan asylum seekers, this paper elaborates on the concept of time in psychodynamic terms, as opposed to the phenomenological, chronologically-based experience of it. My claim is that temporality, as for psychic functioning, is based on non-linear, circular dynamics in which past and present experiences, affects and traumas are in a continuous unconscious dialogue and constantly inform each other, in a way that allows the past to be “retranscribed” in its deep meanings and intimate significance, and the present to acquire enhanced worth and connotations.

adolescents, proper name, identification, humor, joke

We have explored the replacement of proper names with nicknames—the renaming process—from a psychoanalytic perspective. This clinical research was conducted with adolescents in two Latin-American countries. By analyzing participants’ talk during their interactions in gathering places for artistic performance, along with individualized interviews, we approach the symbolic universe surrounding proper names and nicknames. Our work sheds light on how the meanings and signifiers of nicknames impact youth identities, expanding on the “funny” emergence of the social bond and these youngsters’ subjectivity, hereinafter referred to as “par-ceros” (pals; or literally “pair-zero”).

He holds an MA in Ideology and Discourse Analysis from the University of Essex. His research interests span the fields of activism, social movements, and Lacanian psychoanalysis.
activist burnout, fantasy, desire, enjoyment, drive

This essay discusses activist burnout through a Lacanian perspective, focusing on the struggle to heal burnout experienced by activists. It argues that activists find it difficult to heal burnout because of their attachment to the practices that induce burnout, imbued with unconscious desires and enjoyment that help shape their way of life. To illustrate, this essay discusses the fantasy of self-sacrifice and the fantasy of constant action. Drawing on the concepts of traversing the fantasy and drive, the struggle to heal burnout can potentially lead the subject to embrace the satisfaction of struggling to create social change, hence, drive.

Freud, animal studies, Little Hans, Rat Man, Wolf Man

This article explores Freud's original engagement with animal symbols, characters, and stories in his case studies “Little Hans,” “The Rat Man,” and “The Wolf Man.” Employing insights from animal studies, the article examines Freud's views on the human-animal continuum as well as the phenomena of anthropomorphism and zoomorphism, via which human characteristics are affixed to animals and animal characteristics to humans. Also examined is the symbolism surrounding the animals appearing in the fairy tales referenced by Freud's patients, including “Little Red Riding Hood.” We end by considering the contributions that Freud can make to the expanding field of animal studies.

sexuality, social discourse, psychoanalytic treatment, young people, transference, desires

This paper focuses on the impact of ‘society’ on sexuality as represented in the speech of analysands. Despite the fact that western societies are supposedly liberated from taboos and moralistic restriction, there is a paradox in that we often hear young patients speak of the constraints imposed on their sexuality. If the language that surrounds this topic seems to have been, to a great extent, liberated, the intimate expression of desires and individual fantasies often seems hesitant or constrained, we might even say impeded. It is as though there is a need to review intimacy in the light of a collective dictate to liberate oneself, to act, to define or to speak of oneself through sex. Based on the psychoanalytic cure of a young man who suddenly became inhibited in his sexuality, I will demonstrate how additional work may be required around issues of transference and countertransference. This can be most noticeable when the psychoanalyst encounters, or comes up against, a social discourse, when they are in fact desperately seeking a patient's singular narrative, the route of their childhood history and psychosexuality.

sexual addiction, chemsex, autobiography, drive, jouissance, psychoanalysis

In his 2,304 page autobiographical work Journal sexuel d'un garçon d'aujourd'hui, the young author Arthur Dreyfus gives an account of his intense sexual life. This is a life that not only leads to his ‘overdose on sex’, but also propels him into çhemsex – a practice that has spread considerably in recent years within the gay community. This article focuses on the singular narrative of this young man, who tells the reader of his ‘frenetic quest for flesh’ and his furious desire to enjoy, which seems principally encouraged by dating apps. Here, I discuss the subject's relationship to the drive based on current social data, in such a way as to highlight how contemporary setups appear to encourage a frantic search for an unattainable object and an alienating surplus enjoyment (plus-de-jouir). The question of the transgenerational transmission of trauma is considered, bringing to light the deathly fantasies that assail Arthur and lead him to offer himself up to the other's jouissançe. Also discussed is the concept of sexual alienation versus sexual addiction. Finally, I consider how sublimation as an outcome, in so far as it is an alternative to compulsive repetition, can foster the process of resubjectivation through language and the work of analysis.

Based on the two clinical cases of a young adult and an adolescent in psychotherapy, this article reflects on the conscious and unconscious psychological aspects that are implicated in ‘first sexual experiences’. Regardless of the emotional circumstances that surround the actual experience and the way in which they take place, an aggressive, even violent fantasy is very frequently associated with the ‘first time’. This fantasy can complicate or hinder access to a shared sexuality with a partner. This article links such fantasies, on the one hand, to the Oedipal disappointment often experienced when a young person takes their initial step into genital sexuality, and, on the other, to the revival of an infantile sexuality endowed with a sense of separation. The exploration of the violent fantasies and death drive in therapy may facilitate the advent of a more consensual form of engagement with the other.

This film review argues that Paul Preciado's 2023 Orlando: My Political Biography creatively re-envisions Virginia Woolf's 1928 novel Orlando: A Biography in light of contemporary transgender politics. homophobia, internalised homophobia, LGBTQ, sexuality, psychosocial, psychoanalysis

For many members of the LGBTQ community, holding hands with their partners in public, and other public displays of affection (PDAs) is seldom a carefree and spontaneous act. Survey studies have previously indicated that a majority of LGBTQ individuals report that they never hold hands with their partner in public, out of a fear of possible negative or abusive reactions from others. To contribute to qualitative research in this area, in this article we develop an account of the role of homophobia and internalised homophobia in gay men's experience of navigating the act of holding hands with their partners across different landscapes. We take a detailed look at interview material from three study participants to consider the psychic struggles involved when negotiating internal and external barriers to holding hands. The data was generated through photovoice interviews and include verbal as well as visual material. Writing as two psychoanalytic practitioners, we deploy a clinically informed listening stance in our engagement with the study material and offer a distinctly psychosocial theorisation of homophobia.

From a psychoanalytic perspective, this article presents and discusses the concept of interpassivity as a possible unconscious dynamic constitutive of the new forms of contemporary malaise and how it is implicated in the dynamics of subjectivation and enjoyment. Drawing on Mario Perniola's insights into the changing nature of feeling and its radical numbing, the article seeks to connect the threads of this form of malaise by investigating the influence of interpassivity in our relationship with objects and shedding light on the complex interplay between subjectivity and the objects that surround us. Furthermore, the authors propose a reading of interpassive practices that, from within the horizon of contemporary malaise, implies the disappearance of unconscious subjectivity and appears to induce specific processes of desubjectivation.
